chapter_theme: Not wronging the great: their goodwill, once lost, cannot be restored, their anger reaches into any fortress, and their esteem is the only esteem worth having. Time with them is precious, and their bond grows where the bond of the small shrinks.
structure_note: 161, 164 and 168 address a chieftain of hill or shore country, a convention of address. 167 and 168 sit oddly under the chapter heading; neither commentator explains how they belong to it.

161.reading: Do not do what offends even the faultless, counting on them to forgive; once they turn away, no one can undo it.
161.nuance: The warning targets presumption: the very forbearance of the great is what tempts the offence. Pope reads the last line as the great one's mood being hard to change; both commentators read it as the resulting harm being impossible to remove.

162.reading: People of loveless cleverness who have freely gained the company of the great, whom others cannot reach even by paying gold, alas, let the time pass without profit.
162.nuance: Mudaliar takes நயம் as delight or relish, so the fault is an inability to enjoy and draw on what the great offer, not ill will.

163.reading: Disesteem and high esteem alike are for the superior to judge; those versed in refined learning take no account of the scorn or the extravagant praise of the base who know neither grace nor propriety.

164.reading: A brightly hooded snake living in a crevice still dreads the thunder's fury from afar; so those who have angered the great do not escape even inside a fortress hard to reach.

positions.position: The 'great' whose anger cannot be escaped are kings.
The great are elders in general, angered by someone who has wronged them.

164.nuance: Pope reads them as those great in virtue, closer to Shanmuganar. On Mudaliar's reading the fortress is a defence against royal power; on the others, against a moral force no wall can stop.

165.reading: Saying 'you do not know us; there is none like us' is not esteem; esteem is when the worthy who know virtue see one as rare and accept one as great.

166.reading: The friendship of the small dwindles like the morning shadow, while the bond of those of long renown keeps lengthening like the shadow of the declining day.
166.nuance: Mudaliar offers two timings for the shadows (dawn against noon, or forenoon against afternoon); the point, shrinking against growing, is the same either way.

167.reading: Those who keep close enjoy the wealth of kings and the beauty of women, without needing to be worthy; just as cool trees heavy with leaf give shelter alike to all who come near.
167.nuance: The verse states a fact about proximity rather than merit. Under this chapter's heading it may counsel staying near the great, but neither commentator draws that out.

168.reading: Parting even from those who lack discernment brings great, lingering sorrow; so, lord of the long brimming backwaters, not mixing with anyone at all is ten million times better.
168.nuance: This is the renunciant's conclusion drawn from the pain of attachment, and it cuts against the next chapter's praise of good company. Mudaliar spells out the comparison: not joining is better than joining and then parting.

169.reading: Days passed without learning, without going to the great, without giving what one can: if you count them, none such are found among people of good character.

170.reading: The greatness of the great is humility; the fitting quality of one who owns any one excellence is restraint; and, rightly seen, the wealthy are wealthy only if they relieve the distress of those who come to them.
170.nuance: Mudaliar takes ஒன்றிற்கு as any one of learning, wealth or manliness, and records another reading, 'to the Supreme'. Pope narrows it to one science.

links.note: 700 warns a minister that doing improper things on the strength of long familiarity with the king brings ruin. 161 makes the same point about presuming on the forbearance of the great.
896 says one may survive fire but not a lasting offence against the great; 161 says the damage of offending them cannot be undone.
443 calls winning the great the rarest of things. 162 imagines that rarity handed over free and wasted by people who cannot use it.
Both locate worth in the judgment of the worthy. 163 dismisses the verdict of the base, and 165 dismisses one's own verdict on oneself.
895: those who have drawn a fierce king's anger exist nowhere, wherever they go. This matches Mudaliar's reading of 164, where the angered great are kings.
900: even those with overwhelming support perish if the eminent are angered. This matches the reading of 164 in which the great are the morally great and the fortress is no defence.
978 says smallness adorns itself by admiring itself; 165 gives the words of that self-admiration and denies it the name of esteem.
The same claim with a different measure of time: 782 has the waxing and waning moon, 166 the shortening and lengthening shadow.

691 advises those who serve kings to stay neither too near nor too far, like people warming at a fire. 167 observes that those who stay close are the ones who enjoy a king's wealth, without the warning.

839 says, with irony, that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from them brings no pain. 168 says parting even from the undiscerning brings great sorrow. The two make opposite claims about the pain of parting from fools, if தெரிவிலார் is read as fools, as Mudaliar's gloss அறிவிலார் has it.

Both end with கோடி உறும். 816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool, a ranking of companions. 168 drops the ranking: mixing with no one is ten million times better.

168 concludes that not mixing with anyone is far better because of the pain of parting. 174 says no one would hate even painful birth if they could keep friendship with the noble. One makes withdrawal the remedy for life's pain, the other makes companionship the remedy.

Both count days: 38 says letting no day fall idle without good blocks the road of births, and 169 says the good have no day without learning, visiting the great or giving. Both use படாஅ for days that do not occur.
Both define greatness as bowing: பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை in 978, பெரியார் பெருமை சிறுதகைமை in 170.
226 says removing the hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; 170 says only those who relieve their dependants' distress are truly wealthy.

source_issues: 162: Tamil has a corrupted character in கா஢யாரை, read as அரியாரை.
